Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disorder that results in symmetric, inflammatory
arthritis. The immune system spontaneously attacks the synovial lining of joints and tendon
sheaths1 (Resource 1).
The development of disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for rheumatoid arthritis
has decreased the incidence of surgical management, especially in the hand and wrist. Most
studies on surgical treatment in patients with rheumatoid arthritis were performed before
DMARDs2 (Resource 2).
The advent and widespread use of DMARDs has fundamentally transformed this condition and
has, in most patients, decreased the burden of disease, decreased the risk of devastating
musculoskeletal complications, and altered the need for and types of surgical treatment. Many
patients present with minimal rheumatoid joint symptoms; instead, the clinical picture may be
more degenerative or osteoarthritic in nature. Similarly, soft-tissue symptoms (eg, trigger
finger) may more closely approximate those associated with idiopathic conditions.
Regardless, test questions continue to reflect a large number of pre-DMARD scenarios and, in
the rare scenario in which a patient fails to respond to DMARDs or has rheumatoid arthritis
that is unmanaged or undiagnosed, knowledge of the musculoskeletal manifestations of the
disease is essential. Standardized test questions on anti-rheumatoid drugs and when or
whether to withhold and how long to withhold anti-rheumatoid drugs in patients undergoing
surgical treatment also are common.
NSAIDs and corticosteroids are analgesic and anti-inflammatory agents but are not considered
disease-modifying agents.
Biologic and non-biologic DMARDs exist3 (Table 1).

DMARDs are defined as medications that can alter the course of rheumatoid arthritis by
decreasing synovitis and reducing structural damage. The selection of a DMARD is influenced
by the disease severity, drug efficacy versus toxicity profile, route of administration, whether
the patient will reliably take the medications, comorbid conditions, and cost.
Non-biologic DMARDs
Sulfasalazine combines an antimicrobial (sulfapyridine) with salicylate, resulting in a
suppression effect on tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α and interleukin (IL)-1.
Methotrexate, the most widely used DMARD, is effective in 60% to 70% of patients, with a
rapid clinical response (within 6 weeks). It is a folate antagonist that decreases

inflammation by modulating the synthesis of TNF-α; the activity of T-cells; and the
response to inflammatory cytokines, such as IL-1 and IL-6.
Leflunomide, the newest non-biologic DMARD, inhibits the de novo pyrimidine synthesis
required for the proliferation of activated lymphocytes. It also prevents the proliferation
of cluster of differentiation 4 T-cells in patients with early rheumatoid arthritis and inhibits
leukocyte adhesion to vascular endothelium and cytokines (IL-2). Leflunomide is as
effective as methotrexate.4
Biologic DMARDs
Etanercept is a recombinant human TNF receptor fusion protein that binds to circulating
or cell-bound TNF molecules and blocks the action of TNF-α. It is administered
subcutaneously twice a week.
Infliximab is a chimeric murine/human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody that binds to
soluble and membrane-bound TNF and neutralizes the effect of TNF-α. It is administered
via slow intravenous infusion at 0, 2, and 6 weeks initially and every 8 weeks thereafter. It
is used in combination with methotrexate because of better efficacy in disease control.
Adalimumab is a fully human anti-TNF monoclonal antibody administered subcutaneously
every other week.
Adverse events associated with biologic DMARDs are uncommon. They include injection
site reactions (etanercept) and infusion-related adverse effects, such dyspnea, fever,
urticaria (infliximab). Risks of infection, neutropenia, or malignancy (lymphoma) are
associated with these medications.
Anakinra is a recombinant IL-1 antagonist that is capable of occupying the IL receptor
without activating it. Randomized, placebo-controlled trials have demonstrated that
anakinra, alone and in combination with methotrexate, reduces radiological disease
progression.5-7 It also has a favorable risk-benefit profile, producing rapid and sustained
reductions of symptoms with improved quality of life measures.
Hydroxychloroquine has been used to manage rheumatoid arthritis since the 1950s.
Developed as an anti-malarial drug, the mechanism of anti-inflammatory action of
hydroxychloroquine is to inhibit the release of IL-1 and IL-6; however, this is poorly
understood. Treatment response typically is evident within weeks. Although
hydroxychloroquine is associated with a low risk for certain adverse effects (eg, rash, nausea,
maculopathy), its efficacy is exceeded by other DMARDs; therefore, it is not used as
commonly.

Pathologic processes related to rheumatoid arthritis
Subcutaneous nodules are the most common extra-articular manifestations of rheumatoid
arthritis in the upper extremity (20% to 25% of patients).
Dorsal/extensor aspects of the fingers, hand, or elbow
Surgical management is discretionary and largely aesthetic; recurrence is common.2
Whether these nodules are the cause of pain remains unclear.
Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis
Formerly known as juvenile rheumatoid arthritis (Resource 3).
Variable presentation and a broad differential diagnosis9
Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is a lymphocyte-mediated autoimmune disease that affects
children and adolescents.
Systemic JIA is thought to be related to overactivity of phagocytes, which may manifest as
fever, lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly.
A notable percentage of patients with JIA have difficulties with daily life and school because of
hand and wrist symptoms.
Of 121 children (mean age, 13.7 years), 40% reported at least one hand or wrist symptom.10 In
another study, problems with handwriting correlated with pain intensity rather than disease
severity.11
Ultrasonography may detect early synovitis that is not apparent on physical examination.
It also can be used to monitor disease activity.

It is not considered part of the diagnostic criteria of JIA per American College of Rheumatoid
criteria.
On radiographs, carpal joints often are more affected than hand joints.
It may take months to years to establish a diagnosis of JIA.
Clinical and radiographic evaluations at 3- to 6-month intervals are used to monitor
symptoms that may eventually be diagnosed as JIA.
Rheumatoid factor is detected only in patients 8 years or older on presentation; laboratory
tests often are normal in young patients.
Treatment protocols are similar to those for adults with rheumatoid arthritis.
Physical conditioning alleviates joint pain and maintains motion.
Splints and orthoses can address some deformities and alleviate pain.
Bony surgical treatment options, such as arthrodesis and arthroplasty, should be delayed as
much as possible, preferably until skeletal maturity.
Patients with JIA should be referred to an ophthalmologist because of the risk of uveitis
(inflammation of the iris, ciliary, or choroid), which may lead to permanent vision loss.
Extensor Tendon Problems
Tenosynovitis—Inflammation of the tendon sheaths, more specifically extensor tenosynovitis
at the wrist, may be the first sign of rheumatoid arthritis (Resource 4).
Tenosynovitis can invade the substance of the tendon, leading to changes in function and
rarely may result in tendon ruptures.
The most common tendon ruptures involve the extensor digitorum quinti (EDQ) and extensor
digitorum communis (EDC) tendons to the little and ring fingers.
Vaughan-Jackson syndrome is the term used to describe rupture of the extensor tendons
progressing from ulnar (EDQ/EDC to the little finger and then the ring finger) to radial.
Tendon ruptures usually are managed via tendon transfer because direct repair usually is not
possible because of poor tendon quality and retraction. Common tendon transfers for patients
with a Vaughan-Jackson rupture are listed below.
Rupture of the EDQ to the little finger—Consider no tendon transfer but removal of the
offending osteophyte/other causative structure alone if function of little finger extension is
provided by an intact EDC to the little finger.
Rupture of the EDQ to the little finger and the EDC to the little finger: side-to-side transfer,
EDC ring finger to little finger

Extensor Tendon Problems
Tenosynovitis is inflammation of the tendon and synovial sheaths. Three common sites
of tenosynovitis are the dorsal aspect of the wrist, the volar aspect of the wrist, and the
digital flexor tendon sheaths. In the early aspects of disease, synovial tissue remains
thin, and inflammatory fluid distends the tendon sheath. Over time, the synovium
hypertrophies and can adhere to or even invade into the tendon substance. Dorsal
extensor tenosynovitis commonly is one of the first signs of rheumatoid arthritis.
Tenosynovectomy can be considered to aid diagnosis and prevent rupture but is
optional if a good response to DMARDs is observed.
Vaughan-Jackson syndrome is the rupture of the extensor tendons progressing from
ulnar (EDQ/EDC to the little and ring fingers) to radial. The pathoanatomy is based on
distal radioulnar joint involvement, which results in prominence of the ulnar head (caput
ulnae) and or associated osteophytes. This prominence leads to attritional extensor
tendon rupture over time. Management of radial deviation and supination of the carpus
can be addressed via extensor carpi radialis longus to extensor carpi ulnaris transfer to
supplement ulnar deviation strength; however, little information is available about the
long-term success of such procedures in prevention of recurrence. In patients with
degenerative arthritis, concomitant arthrodesis may be considered. Tendon ruptures
often are managed via side-to-side suturing to intact EDC tendons, which has been
shown to be biomechanically superior to Pulvertaft weave. If several tendons are
ruptured, flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) tendon transfer may be considered. Distal
ulna resection or osteophyte excision is necessary to prevent rupture of the transferred

Dorsal tenosynovectomy with or without tendon repair usually involves a straight,
midline incision over the dorsal aspect of the wrist. The extensor retinaculum is exposed
and divided obliquely (or Z-lengthened) for later repair. Inflamed tenosynovium is
removed, and ruptured tendons are sewn to adjacent intact tendons/tendon transfers. If
the extensor retinaculum is split, the distal part can be placed volar to the tendons for
protection. The proximal half of the retinaculum is then sutured dorsally to prevent
bowstringing in an unfused wrist. Often, this tissue is of poor quality and cannot
effectively perform this function. Tenosynovitis recurrence rates have been as high as
10% before DMARDs.1,2,13
Differential diagnosis of inability to extend the digits includes extensor tendon
rupture (absence of tenodesis with wrist flexion), ulnar subluxation of the extensor
tendon at the metacarpophalangeal (MCP) joint (able to hold the finger straight after
passively extended to correct the subluxation), and posterior interosseous nerve
palsy.
Flexor Tendon Problems
Flexor tenosynovitis in the carpal tunnel may cause median neuropathy (Resource 5).
Flexor tendons can rupture because of attrition related to bony prominence.
Flexor pollicis longus (FPL) rupture caused by a scaphoid spur is the most common rupture
(Mannerfelt lesion).
FPL rupture: FDS transfer or tendon graft with spur excision
FPL rupture with advanced disease: interphalangeal joint arthrodesis
FDS ruptures in the digits: observation if preserved FDP function
FDP ruptures in the digits: synovectomy and distal interphalangeal (DIP) joint fusion if the
FDS is functioning
In the digits, crepitation with motion may be present.
Nonsurgical management
Splinting of the hand and fingers in intrinsic plus position

Flexor Tendon Problems
Hypertrophic synovium of the flexor tendon sheath may present as median nerve
compression at the carpal tunnel. Findings can be confirmed via physical examination
and nerve conduction studies. Some temporary relief may be afforded by corticosteroid
injections or DMARDs; however, surgical management via transverse carpal ligament
release and flexor tenosynovectomy often is indicated. Some surgeons recommend
separating the flexor digitorum profundus (FDP) and the FDS en masse based on the
rationale that dissecting each of the four distinct FDP tendons to individual digits may
contribute to postoperative adhesions. Other surgeons find it easier to perform
synovectomy one tendon at a time. The floor of the carpal tunnel should be explored
and débrided of any bony prominences, which most commonly are present at the volar
scaphoid.
The most common tendon at risk is the FPL tendon, and rupture because of a volar
scaphoid spur is referred to as a Mannerfelt lesion. The FPL should be repaired or
reconstructed, and the spur in question should be excised.1,2,14
Flexor tenosynovectomy: The approach usually is a Brunner zig-zag incision. Key aspects
of this procedure include preservation of the pulley system to prevent ulnar/radial drift
and bowstringing. The diseased tendon sheath is excised between the pulleys. To
decrease the overall contents of the digital flexor sheath, the ulnar slip of the FDS can be
resected to help counteract any ulnar deviating force. The tendons should track better,
and this method has been shown to reduce recurrence and revision surgery rates during
this procedure with appropriate postoperative range of motion protocols. Any nodules
within the tendon itself should be excised and closed with the use of a fine running
suture. The FDP is more prone to nodules than the FDS. Before DMARDs, flexor
synovectomies were not thought to be as successful as extensor synovectomies because
of recurrence as high as 30%. Patients with inflammatory arthritis occasionally present
with a trigger digit. Historically, incision of the A1 pulley was relatively contraindicated

Radiocarpal Joint
Erosion of the palmar side of the distal radius, the scaphoid waist, and the triquetrum
are common. The disease attenuates major wrist ligaments, including the palmar
radiocarpal, scapholunate, and lunotriquetral ligaments. Ligament insufficiency may
contribute to carpal malalignment, typically named for the angulation of the lunate,
either dorsal or volar (dorsal and volar intercalated segment instability).15

Radioscapholunate arthrodesis may offer pain relief and stabilization with some
preservation of wrist range of motion. The procedure is performed via a dorsal approach
to the wrist. The radiocarpal and midcarpal joints are explored to ensure that partial
arthrodesis is indicated. The radiocarpal joint is denuded of cartilage and positioned
against the lunate fossa of the distal radius. Local autograft or allograft can be used to
aid in fusion. The position of the lunate should be neutral (with special considerations to
correct the rheumatoid wrist deformities). Fixation can be achieved with the use of
Kirschner wires, staples, screws, or plates16 (Video 1).

several types of pathophysiology: extensor subluxation (sagittal band attenuation), collateral
ligament attenuation, volar plate attenuation, and deformity at the wrist (radial deviation)
(Figure 2).

Type I or boutonnière thumb (most common)
MCP joint flexion with compensatory hyperextension of the interphalangeal joint
Alternative mechanisms
EPL rupture
FPL rupture with a concurrent volar plate injury
Management of type I injuries
If the MCP and interphalangeal joints are flexible, then synovectomy of the MCP joint with
reconstruction of the extensor mechanism may be adequate.
If the MCP joint becomes stiff and painful with degenerative changes, a bony procedure,
such as an arthrodesis or arthroplasty, can be performed.
Type II rheumatoid arthritis thumb deformity is rare. The clinical presentation is the same as
that of type I; however, the etiology is from trapeziometacarpal subluxation. Management is
similar to treatment options already described.
Type III, swan neck deformity.
MCP joint hyperextension, interphalangeal joint flexion, and metacarpal adduction.
Management: trapeziometacarpal joint arthroplasty or arthrodesis
If the deformity is fixed at the MCP joint, MCP joint surgery similar to that described in the
management of type I may be required.
Type IV deformity (gamekeeper thumb)
Ulnar collateral ligament and volar plate are attenuated and lax because of synovitis.
Radial proximal phalanx deviation and compensatory metacarpal adduction
Long-term metacarpal adduction may lead to contractures of the first dorsal interosseus
and adductor pollicis muscles.
Management: arthrodesis of the thumb MCP joint
Type V deformity involves isolated disruption of the MCP joint volar plate with resulting
hyperextension deformity. A flexion deformity of the interphalangeal joint develops. This
deformity also should be managed via arthrodesis, especially if joint degeneration is present.
The last type of deformity is arthritis mutilans, which is extension destruction of the joint and
is managed via arthrodesis with or without bone grafting.2,15,21

MCP Joints
The joint in the hand most affected by rheumatoid arthritis is the MCP joint. The
pathology begins as a proliferative synovitis and progresses to volar subluxation and
ulnar deviation. The normal synovial membrane is on the periphery of the cartilage, with
extensions volarly and dorsally (at which it is largest). Rheumatoid synovitis affects the
static and dynamic stabilizers of the MCP joint. Ulnar deviation likely results from the
asymmetry of the metacarpal head because the radial aspect of the metacarpal head is
larger than the ulnar side. In addition, the carpal bone collapse and deformity lead to
radial deviation of the wrist with subsequent compensatory ulnar deviation of the MCP
joints. The radial sagittal band is weaker than the ulnar sagittal band; therefore,
attenuation of the radial sagittal band may contribute to ulnar drift of the fingers. If the
extensor tendons subluxate volarly or rupture, the unopposed pull of the flexor tendons
may contribute to volar subluxation of the proximal phalanx. Synovial proliferation
results in attenuation of accessory collaterals and the membranous volar plate with
ulnar shift of the flexor sheath. The synovitis also leads to intrinsic muscle contractures,
which contributes to proximal phalanx volar subluxation.2
The pathology begins with synovitis at the MCP joint, which relaxes the extensor
mechanism of the thumb (dorsal capsule, extensor pollicis brevis, and extensor hood).
With time, this stretching causes the formation of an extensor lag as the hood becomes
incompetent. The resultant deformity is MCP joint flexion and a displacement of the
extensor pollicis longus (EPL) more ulnarly. This MCP joint flexion causes compensatory
abduction of the thumb metacarpal radially. As the EPL subluxates, the insertion on the
distal phalanx is under tension, causing a hyperextension effect. These deformities are

The prevalence of psoriatic arthritis is approximately 0.02% to 0.25% in the general
population. Familial and twin studies suggest a genetic connection and relationships to
environmental factors (trauma, infection, HIV, etc.). The dermal-epidermal junction and
tendon-bone interfaces are areas of high-stress that are susceptible to inflammatory
infiltrate. Similar to rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis also results in synovitis and
upregulation of inflammatory markers, such as TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6, and IL-13.28

arthritis. Initial therapy includes NSAIDs and traditional DMARDs, such as methotrexate,
sulfasalazine, and leflunomide, which are initiated early. If inflammation persists despite
management, more intensive management via TNF-α inhibitors is indicated. Newer
biologic treatment options help prevent radiologic progression of peripheral arthritis
and manage digital symptoms, such as dactylitis and nail lesions. Some studies show
that these TNF-α inhibitors, such as etanercept, may be cost-effective early.

relief and function.29 Factors associated with surgical management included
radiographic severity, number of joints involved, and the duration of the disease process
but not laboratory values. In another study, 24% of patients with psoriatic arthritis
underwent hand surgery, which is notably higher than numbers reported for total knee
arthroplasty, total hip arthroplasty, and foot and ankle surgery.30

Erosive Osteoarthritis
Erosive osteoarthritis is a disease, limited to the hand, that involves the interphalangeal
joints of the fingers, most commonly the DIP joint. The term was coined by Peter et al33
in 1966. Symptoms are more common in women than men (female to male ratio of
approximately 10:1). The index and middle fingers are more frequently involved than the
ring finger or the little finger. A firm definition of this disease in the literature is lacking;
therefore, little information is available on diagnosis and management. Some studies
describe that as many as 40% of patients with classic osteoarthritis have some similar
erosive changes.21,34 Therefore, many consider erosive osteoarthritis to be a subset of
osteoarthritis.
The pathology is episodic, with cyclic destruction of bone with intermittent repair and
remodeling. These episodic flare-ups are associated with pain, swelling, erythema, and
limited function of the interphalangeal joints of the hands. Patients present with
considerable pain and functional limitations. The overall pathophysiology is similar to
rheumatoid arthritis or psoriatic arthritis, with the caveat that erosive osteoarthritis is
not a systemic disease.

Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is atypical proliferation of the skin, soft tissue, and bone of the

Gout is the clinical syndrome that results from an inflammatory response to
monosodium urate crystals. Hyperuricemia (serum urate >2 standard deviations from
the mean) is related to gout; however, it is not diagnostic. The urate builds from
ingesting foods containing purine or increased endogenous synthesis. Humans lack an
enzyme uricase (present in other mammals), allowing them to build more urate than
other animals. The presentation typically is monoarticular. Microscopically, a tophus
consists of a collection of urate crystals with inflammatory cells and some signs of
necrosis. Macroscopically, tophi are liquid, solid, or in a paste-like semifluid state in
between liquid and solid. The semifluid state is thought to contribute to pain.

decreased urate solubility. Gout of the DIP joints of the fingers is common in elderly
individuals, who often have underlying arthritic changes. Older women specifically have
increased arthritis at baseline. This, in combination with the increased use of diuretics in
this patient population, predisposes patients to gouty attacks. Acute attacks may mimic
infection. In the hand, flexor tendons tend to be more commonly affected, and patients
may present with tenosynovitis, tendon rupture, contracture, or even nerve
compression. If the extensor tendons are involved, typically this occurs at the level of the
MCP joints. Gout of the wrist may present in a manner similar to that of septic arthritis
(Resource 13).

Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease (Pseudogout,
Chondrocalcinosis)
Calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease (or pseudogout/chondrocalcinosis) is a crystal
deposition disease that often is similar to gouty arthritis in presentation and can be incited
because of trauma (Resource 14).
Calcification of triangular fibrocartilage and isolated scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal joint disease
are specific for calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease.37
Diagnosis
Polarized light microscopy of joint aspirate demonstrates rod-shaped, weakly positive
birefringent pyrophosphate crystals.
Radiographs demonstrate degenerative joint disease and specifically calcification in the knee
meniscus or the triangular fibrocartilage complex.
The differential diagnosis for calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease includes
osteoarthritis, gouty arthritis, and infection. Joint aspiration often is indicated if concern for
infection exists.
Management usually is nonsurgical; however, surgical treatment may be useful in patients
with specific joint involvement.

Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition Disease (Pseudogout,
Chondrocalcinosis)
The etiology of the disease may be sporadic; however, some evidence shows that it is
inherited because of increased expression of the ANK gene, which leads to a buildup of
inorganic pyrophosphate. This is a substrate for crystal formation in aged cartilage.
Crystals first appear in the synovial fluid and are then deposited into the synovial
membrane, wrist ligaments, and articular cartilage. Typically, patients present between
50 and 59 years and may have a range of presentations from asymptomatic to severe
deformity. Often, patients have pain, swelling, and decreased range of motion in the
wrist. Trauma can incite an acute flare of previously asymptomatic disease. Both wrists
are affected in most patients.

Classic features include isolated scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal joint disease and calcification
of the triangular fibrocartilage. Pseudotumors can form and compress the carpal tunnel.
The scapholunate, distal radioulnar, lunotriquetral, midcarpal, radiolunate, and
pisotriquetral joints may be involved.
Radiographic signs include degenerative joint changes, with calcification of the triangular
fibrocartilage complex, scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal, distal radioulnar, and other joints.
Knee radiographs may demonstrate evidence of meniscal calcification. Polarized light
microscopy of affected joint aspirate may show rod-shaped, weakly positive birefringent
pyrophosphate crystals (compared with gout).
Nonsurgical management via splint immobilization, NSAIDs, and intra-articular steroid
injections usually is sufficient. For recurrent disease, prophylaxis with colchicine may be
helpful. For specific areas of degeneration, surgical treatment similar to that for
osteoarthritis may be helpful. Typically, these are arthrodesis or arthroplasty
procedures.
